verses.text: So Israel set out with all that he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
And that night God spoke to Israel in a vision: "Jacob, Jacob!" He said. "Here I am," replied Jacob.
"I am God," He said, "the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there.
I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph's own hands will close your eyes."
Then Jacob departed from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel took their father Jacob in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him, along with their children and wives.
They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt.
Jacob took with him to Egypt his sons and grandsons, and his daughters and granddaughters—all his offspring.
Now these are the names of the sons of Israel (Jacob and his descendants) who went to Egypt: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah born to Jacob in Paddan-aram, in addition to his daughter Dinah. The total number of sons and daughters was thirty-three.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
The children of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
These are the sons of Jacob born to Zilpah—whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah—sixteen in all.
The sons of Jacob's wife Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph in the land of Egypt by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are the sons of Rachel born to Jacob—fourteen in all.
The son of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the sons of Jacob born to Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel—seven in all.
All those belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt—his direct descendants, besides the wives of Jacob's sons—numbered sixty-six persons.
And with the two sons who had been born to Joseph in Egypt, the members of Jacob's family who went to Egypt were seventy in all.
Now Jacob had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When Jacob's family arrived in the land of Goshen,
Joseph prepared his chariot and went there to meet his father Israel. Joseph presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!"
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and inform Pharaoh: 'My brothers and my father's household from the land of Canaan have come to me.
The men are shepherds; they raise livestock, and they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own.'
When Pharaoh summons you and asks, 'What is your occupation?'

you are to say, 'Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth—both we and our fathers.' Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians."

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 to 50)
context.audience: Israel, the twelve tribes, learning how their fathers came down to Egypt and how God turned evil to good
context.setting: Israel sets out with everything he has, and at Beersheba he offers sacrifices to “the God of his father Isaac” (v.1). That night God speaks: “Jacob, Jacob!… Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there. I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph’s own hands will close your eyes” (vv.2-4). Jacob’s sons carry him in Pharaoh’s wagons with their wives, children and flocks (vv.5-7). The chapter lists the family, son by son and grandson by grandson, “seventy in all” counting Joseph and his sons (vv.8-27). Judah goes ahead to get directions to Goshen (v.28). Joseph drives out in his chariot, and when he sees his father he “embraced him, and wept profusely” (v.29). “Finally I can die,” says Israel, “now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” (v.30). Joseph coaches his brothers to tell Pharaoh they are herdsmen, so that they will be settled apart in Goshen, “since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians” (vv.31-34).
context.custom: Seventy is a round number of fullness; the table of nations in Genesis 10 also lists about seventy peoples, and Israel enters Egypt as a whole people in miniature. The Greek translation of the Old Testament counts seventy-five, and Stephen follows it (Acts 7:14). Egyptian farmers of the Nile valley looked down on the herders who drifted in from the eastern deserts. A painting at Beni Hasan of about 1890 BC shows a group of Asiatic men, women and children, with donkeys and goods, arriving in Egypt to trade.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 47: Jacob meets Pharaoh, the family settles in Goshen, and Joseph manages Egypt through the worst of the famine.
context.timelineBible: This is the last time God speaks in Genesis, and He speaks as He spoke to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob before: “Do not be afraid… I will go down with you” (vv.3-4). The promise of a great nation will be fulfilled in Egypt (Exodus 1:7), and “I will surely bring you back” in the exodus. Abraham was told his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own for four hundred years (Genesis 15:13).

translation.meaning: To go down. Going down to Egypt is always “down” in Genesis; God promises to go down with Jacob and bring him up again (v.4).
A nation, a people. The promise to Abraham, “I will make you into a great nation” (12:2), will be fulfilled in Egypt.
Seventy, ten times seven: a full number. Seventy persons go down to Egypt; Exodus 1:5 begins with the same count.

overview.discussion: God told Jacob, “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt… I will go down with you” (vv.3-4). What unknown place am I afraid to go, and does God’s promise to go with me change that?

historicalImage.caption: The procession of the Aamu, Asiatic visitors from Canaan, painted in the tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan (about 1890 BC). Men, women and children in bright woven robes come into Egypt with donkeys, as Jacob’s family did (Genesis 46:5-7).
